questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What a decision needs besides a body of evidence
questions.learningObjective: name the element a record of evidence cannot supply
questions.stem: A group has assembled everything the record holds about where a service should be sited. What does that record still fail to supply?

options.text: A further round of evidence, since no amount of investigation removes the need for a criterion
options.misconception: assumes more evidence is the missing ingredient and so makes the search never terminate

options.text: A majority among the members, since a criterion cannot be applied until the group votes on it
options.misconception: substitutes a vote for the missing criterion and treats agreement as the standard

options.text: A criterion against which the candidate sites are compared, since evidence narrows the field without choosing in it
A single figure to weigh everything by, since several criteria cannot be compared with each other
options.misconception: insists on one number and overlooks that criteria can be weighed and argued separately

questions.explanation: Evidence describes the options; it does not choose between them. A file can establish that one site has cleaner water, another has the shorter road and a third is the only one with room to expand, and every one of those facts can be true while the decision is still open. What closes it is a criterion: a stated standard saying how much each consideration is worth against the others. That criterion can be argued for, revised or rejected, and none of that is supplied by finding out more about the same three sites, because the gap is between what is the case and what matters more.
questions.hint: Ask whether the file settles how much one good is worth against another.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A total that ranks the option already in use
questions.learningObjective: read what a weighted criteria table settles and what it leaves open

stimulus.kind: criteria table written for this question
stimulus.body: Scoring sheet written for this exercise, produced by a service group choosing between three arrangements for its records. 'Four criteria are scored from 1 to 5, where 5 is best, and the four scores are added with equal weight. Keep what we do now scores 5, 1, 5, 5 and totals 16. Move to a fully electronic file scores 2, 5, 3, 2 and totals 12. A partial upgrade scores 3, 3, 4, 4 and totals 14. The four criteria, in order, are one-off setup cost, speed of retrieval, control of who may see a record, and retraining burden.'

questions.stem: The group has published these totals. What do the totals establish about the choice?

options.text: That the electronic file should be chosen, since the criterion it wins by the largest margin is the one that matters most
options.misconception: treats the widest single margin as decisive while the other three margins run the opposite way and are larger together

options.text: That the partial upgrade is the sound compromise, since an option between two extremes carries less risk than either
options.misconception: picks the middle option on the ground of moderation, which is not among the criteria and not in the sheet

options.text: That the totals should be discarded, since adding scores across different criteria does not produce a quantity
options.misconception: dismisses aggregation altogether and leaves the group with no comparison of any kind

options.text: That keeping the present arrangement ranks first under equal weighting, and the sheet says nothing about whether these four criteria are the right ones

questions.explanation: Under equal weighting the present arrangement totals 16, the partial upgrade 14 and the electronic file 12, so the sheet ranks the option that changes nothing first and the full change last. The arithmetic is worth doing carefully because it settles only what it measures: the present arrangement leads on setup cost by 3, on control of access by 2 and on retraining by 3, an advantage of 8, while the electronic file leads on retrieval by 4. Retrieval would have to carry more than twice the weight of the other three for that lead to overtake the other three. That is a claim about the weights and not about the arrangements, and the sheet never argues for its own criteria, which is why the ranking is a statement about how the group has chosen to score rather than a verdict on what to do.
questions.hint: Add the margins in both directions and ask which one the sheet decided in advance to count.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What changing a weight changes in a comparison
questions.learningObjective: distinguish a change of weight from a change of measurement
questions.stem: In a comparison of options, one criterion is given more weight than the rest. What has the group then changed?

options.text: The accuracy of the scores, since a better-measured criterion deserves more weight than a poorly measured one
options.misconception: assumes weight follows measurement quality, which is a separate argument about the instrument

options.text: The trade-off being made, since a weight states how much one good is worth against another and the totals move with it
The number of criteria, since a criterion counted twice is the same as having two criteria
options.misconception: conflates weight with repetition and expects the score to be counted as though it appeared twice

options.text: The set of options, since a heavily weighted criterion is the one an option has to meet
options.misconception: turns a weight into a qualification and expects heavy weight to remove options rather than favour them

questions.explanation: A weight is a statement of relative worth: it says how much a gain on one criterion offsets a loss on another, and every total in the table is recomputed when it changes. That is a change to the group's answer to a question it had not been asked, namely what matters more and by how much. The measurement quality of a score is a separate matter, settled by asking how the scores were produced; treating a score as better made does not make it more important. Nor does doubling a weight add a criterion, because the comparison still runs over four rows. And a weight does not remove an option, since an option that fails a weighted criterion still scores and still appears in the total.
questions.hint: Ask what a weight is a number of, and whether anything is measured differently after it changes.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A threshold that turns a measurement into an act
questions.learningObjective: separate a trigger for acting from a judgement about the thing acted on
questions.stem: A service is reviewed only when the number of recorded problems about it reaches a stated level. What does that level do?

options.text: It makes the tally more trustworthy, since small numbers of reports are not worth measuring at all
options.misconception: treats the level as a filter on the quality of the count rather than on when to act

options.text: It settles whether the service is good, since the level at which review begins is a verdict on the service
options.misconception: reads a trigger for looking as though it were a judgement about what is looked at

options.text: It converts a running tally into a point for acting, so the group moves when a line is crossed rather than when the change is judged large enough
It removes the need for judgement, since a number agreed in advance settles every later case
options.misconception: believes that fixing a figure beforehand removes judgement from everything that follows it

questions.explanation: A threshold is a decision rule attached to a measurement: it says at what point on the scale the group does something rather than continues to count. Once it is crossed the group still has to decide what the level means, whether the rise is real and what to do, so nothing about the service has been settled by the crossing itself. Fixing the figure beforehand is a genuine virtue, since it removes the temptation to move the line after the result is known, but it settles when to look and not what is there. A count of one and a count of nine both fail to tell the group whether the service is good, and a threshold set at three tells them only when to start asking.
questions.hint: Ask what has to happen after the line is crossed.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Costs that differ across the settings where the same evidence is used
questions.learningObjective: explain why a threshold on evidence depends on what each error costs
questions.stem: Two procedures rest on evidence of equal strength. In one, a false alarm cancels a treatment that was likely to help. In the other, a missed case is followed by serious harm. What follows from that difference?

options.text: Nothing follows, since evidence strong enough for one of these procedures is strong enough for both
options.misconception: treats the strength of the evidence as the whole of a threshold and holds the consequences irrelevant

options.text: The same evidence can support acting in one setting and waiting in the other, since whether it is enough depends on what each kind of error costs
Waiting is right wherever a false alarm does harm, since waiting is the option that can be taken back
options.misconception: assumes reversibility settles the question and passes over what the waiting itself costs

options.text: The evidence must be stronger in the second setting, since only the consequences differ and the question is settled the same way twice
options.misconception: separates the strength of evidence from the cost of error and so varies one without touching the other

questions.explanation: How much evidence a decision needs is always relative to what being wrong will cost. The same false alarm rate that is unacceptable where a harm follows can be perfectly acceptable where the cost is a cancelled benefit already counted, because the two procedures are not asking the same question of the evidence. This is why a rule stating a required confidence level must also state what it is protecting, and why a level that works in one setting is not automatically portable to another. Reversibility is a real consideration but it is one consideration among the costs rather than a rule that always decides, since a delay that is reversible can also cost the thing the decision was for.
questions.hint: Ask what being wrong costs in each setting before asking how strong the evidence is.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A procedure that treats every decision alike
questions.learningObjective: identify the assumption a uniform checking rule rests on
questions.stem: A group's procedure requires the same amount of checking for every decision it takes. What is that rule assuming about the decisions it governs?

options.text: That they are equally hard to undo and equally consequential, which is an assumption about them rather than about the checking
That checking costs nothing, so treating every decision alike is the fairest arrangement available
options.misconception: justifies uniform checking by fairness and leaves the cost of checking out of the account

options.text: That the members agree on how much care each decision deserves, which one uniform rule spares them from arguing about
options.misconception: hides the weighting decision inside a rule that looks neutral and so never gets argued about

options.text: That no decision matters more than another, which is what treating them all in the same way is meant to express
options.misconception: takes the uniformity as the conclusion instead of as an assumption still to be tested

questions.explanation: One rule applied to every decision is a decision about how much care each decision deserves, made once and applied everywhere. That works only if the decisions are alike in the respects that matter, and they rarely are: a booking of a room and a change to what the service is for sit at opposite ends of both reversibility and consequence. The rule is attractive precisely because it looks neutral and saves an argument, and that is the problem, since an unexamined weighting never gets examined. The repair is small and does not need a different rule for every case: separate the decisions into bands, say which band gets how much checking, and let the bands be argued over.
questions.hint: Ask what a rule that applies everywhere has already decided.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What irreversibility licenses in a choice
questions.learningObjective: state what follows from a difference in how far a decision can be undone
questions.stem: Two decisions look similar in what they are expected to achieve, but one can be undone in a month and the other cannot be undone at all. What does that difference license?

options.text: A difference in how far the group should press before committing, since an irreversible choice deserves more evidence rather than more confidence
A decision not to commit, since an irreversible choice is one a group ought in general to refuse
options.misconception: turns irreversibility into a veto and so rules out choices that are sometimes right

options.text: Nothing, since whether a decision can be undone affects how it is carried out rather than whether to take it
options.misconception: confines reversibility to implementation and denies that it belongs in the threshold

options.text: The opposite decision, since an irreversible choice should be taken against whatever can be undone
options.misconception: inverts the caution that irreversibility warrants and ends up recommending the safer option for the wrong reason

questions.explanation: Reversibility is a property of the choice and it changes how much has to be known before the choice is made, not whether it may be made. Where a decision can be undone, a wrong call costs the effort of reversing and the group can learn at relatively little expense, so a modest case may be enough. Where it cannot be undone, the same modest case is not enough, because the remedy after the fact is only compensation and not the thing lost. That argues for holding out for more evidence rather than for more confidence, and the distinction matters because confidence is a feeling about a case while evidence is the case. It does not make every irreversible choice wrong, since plenty of things can be done only once and the alternative to an irreversible act is often a delay that is itself costly.
questions.hint: Ask what a wrong call costs where the group can put things back and where it cannot.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: The option a choice removes
questions.learningObjective: identify what a comparison of two courses leaves out
questions.stem: A group compares two courses of action by listing what each will cost and what each will produce. What has that comparison left out?

options.text: The direct costs, since those are the figures that can actually be measured and compared
options.misconception: admits only measurable costs into the comparison and quietly drops the rest

options.text: The effect on other groups, which belongs to a later decision rather than to this one
options.misconception: defers the distributional question instead of noticing that the trade-off has already been made

options.text: The worth of the course not taken, because choosing one of them is also giving up what the other would have produced
The time the comparison itself consumes, which is a cost of the same kind as the others
options.misconception: adds a third element to the list and leaves the forgone alternative unexamined

questions.explanation: Every choice forecloses, and a comparison that tabulates only the two options in play omits the value of what choosing either of them gives up. That is not a small gap: the forgone course is frequently the one whose benefits are harder to write down, and a comparison which leaves it out will drift towards whichever option is easiest to tabulate. The difficulty is not that the value is unknowable but that it has to be put on the same footing as the costs, which means asking what the group would most regret not having done. The effort of making the comparison is a real cost and a small one beside that, and the effects on other groups are a further entry of the same kind rather than a separate matter.
questions.hint: Ask what is given up by the act of choosing, not only by the option chosen.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Counting the cost of leaving things as they are
questions.learningObjective: state what has to be added before inaction counts as an option
questions.stem: A group describes its plan as doing nothing until a review has finished. What must be added before that counts as one option among the others?

options.text: A price for it, since leaving the arrangement as it stands has consequences that keep accumulating while the review runs
A majority in favour, since doing nothing is a real option only if most members accept it
options.misconception: makes the standing arrangement depend on assent rather than on what it produces

options.text: A deadline, since an option with no end date is a postponement rather than a decision
options.misconception: supplies timing as the missing element when the gap is the accumulating cost of waiting

options.text: An alternative to stand beside, since doing nothing is not a choice between courses of action
options.misconception: rules inaction out by category instead of asking what it costs to keep waiting

questions.explanation: Doing nothing is one of the options and it has consequences like any other: the arrangement continues to produce its costs, the delay itself consumes time, and the group is not choosing between a course and nothing but between a course and a continuation. A continuation that is described in a sentence and never costed will almost always look cheaper than a course with a price tag, and that appearance is an artefact of how the sheet was written. Putting a figure on the continuation is not always possible, and when it is not the honest form is to say what the delay forgoes and by roughly how much, so that the comparison can be argued rather than settled by presentation.
questions.hint: Ask what the delay itself produces while the review runs.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Certain, probable and possible consequences
questions.learningObjective: say what would make a claim of near-certainty assessable
questions.stem: A proposal is defended on the ground that it will almost certainly improve things. What would make that defence something the group could assess?

options.text: A larger trial, since only more data can separate the three and settle which will happen
options.misconception: assumes the categories can only be told apart by gathering further data

options.text: Someone to contest the claim, since a claim of this kind is settled by being argued against
options.misconception: looks for a counter-voice where what is needed is a way of stating the claim precisely

options.text: A statement of what is certain, what is probable and what is only possible, since each of the three carries a different warrant
A longer list of benefits, since the more benefits are on the table the more certain the improvement is
options.misconception: takes the number of claimed benefits as their warrant and never asks how likely each is

questions.explanation: Almost certainly flattens three different things into one word. Some consequences follow from the arrangement whatever else happens, some are likely given what the group knows, and some are merely available, in the sense that the change makes them more possible without doing anything to make them likely. A decision can properly rest on the first and be argued about on the second, while the third belongs in a list of what the group is accepting a risk of rather than in the case for the change. More data may help settle which is which, but a claim about certainty is also defeated by being stated properly, since the group cannot tell what has not been separated while it is all called certain.
questions.hint: Ask how many different claims are hidden inside the word almost certainly.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: An effect produced through another party response
questions.learningObjective: read a consultation paper that counts sessions rather than users

stimulus.kind: consultation paper written for this question
stimulus.body: Consultation paper written for this exercise, about a community hall run by a town council. 'The council proposes to close the hall on weekday evenings and to open it on Saturdays instead. Evening sessions affected in the coming year: 60. Saturday sessions that would be offered in their place: 50. Two groups use the hall in the evening. A youth group that meets on Thursday evenings says its members could come on a Saturday. A language class that meets on Tuesday evenings says its members could not, because several of them work shifts that finish late on Saturdays.'

questions.stem: What does this paper establish about the effect on the hall and its users?

options.text: That 10 evening sessions a year are lost outright, and that of the two groups that have spoken only one reports being able to use the Saturday replacement
That the change costs the hall nothing, since 50 of the 60 affected sessions are being offered again on another day
options.misconception: counts the offered replacement as a session that already exists and so adds 50 to the 50 that remain

options.text: That both groups will be equally affected, since both meet on weekday evenings and the proposal treats them alike
options.misconception: assumes a uniform effect on users whose availability for the replacement day was described differently

options.text: That the language class should be given the ten surplus sessions, since it is the group the paper leaves with nothing
options.misconception: turns the size of the shortfall into an entitlement the paper neither offers nor rules out

questions.explanation: The paper counts sessions, and the difference between the two numbers is 10 sessions a year that are removed with nothing offered in their place. The session count is not the effect, because the two groups in the hall are affected differently: one reports being able to use a Saturday and one reports being unable to, so for that group the whole of the Tuesday and Thursday evening use is at risk and none of the 50 offered sessions reaches it. The paper therefore supports a claim about the shortfall and about who can reach the replacement, and it does not support a claim that the change is costless. Equally, nothing in it decides that the language class is owed the ten, which is a question the paper never raises and a question the council would have to answer.
questions.hint: Subtract the offered sessions from the affected ones, then ask who can actually reach them.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A difficulty a decision moves rather than settles
questions.learningObjective: decide what to ask next when a measure improves and another worsens
questions.stem: A scheme is introduced to shorten a long queue, and the queue falls while complaints about the service rise. What should the group ask next?

options.text: Whether the complaints are justified, since a rise in complaints is itself a verdict on the scheme
options.misconception: treats a change in complaint volume as a judgement rather than as a sign of where the problem went

options.text: Where the demand went, since a queue that shortens by being redirected leaves the difficulty standing somewhere else
Whether the queue really fell, since a queue falling and complaints rising cannot both be true of one service
options.misconception: assumes that two measures of the same service have to move in the same direction

options.text: How to reduce the complaints, since a scheme cannot fairly be judged by the people it should serve better
options.misconception: classifies disapproving feedback as noise to be managed rather than as information about the scheme

questions.explanation: A queue is a waiting count, and waiting can be reduced by moving the difficulty rather than by removing it: by turning people away at the door, by making them ask a different office, by asking them to bring documents they will be sent home for, or by making the queue shorter and the service worse. Complaints rising while waiting falls is the pattern that should make the group look for that, and the question to ask is where the demand went rather than whether it was served. The two measures are not in contradiction, since a service can shorten a queue and produce more complaints at the same time, and neither is a verdict on its own: a rise in complaints may be a sign that people are being made to do more work themselves.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to the people who are no longer waiting.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: The part of a question a decision deliberately leaves open
questions.learningObjective: explain what separating a decision into stages actually buys
questions.stem: A group decides where to site a facility but not how it should be run. What does that division of the question buy the group?

options.text: Freedom from being wrong about the running, since the group has committed itself to nothing about how it operates
options.misconception: supposes that leaving a question undecided protects the group from being wrong about it

options.text: A decision that can be made while a harder disagreement is still open, since the two need never be settled at the same sitting
A decision that can be undone cheaply later, since only the site was committed and the running can follow
options.misconception: assumes that deferring part of a choice makes the whole choice cheap to reverse

options.text: A decision nobody can object to, since the part most likely to be disputed has been set aside for later
options.misconception: confuses deferring a disagreement with having removed it

questions.explanation: Splitting a decision in two is a way of sequencing a disagreement, and the gain is real: where a site can be chosen without settling how the thing will be operated, a group with a genuine disagreement about the operation can still make progress on the site and hold the harder question for a meeting that has more to work with. Two things do not follow. Leaving the second part open does not protect anyone from being wrong about it, because the operation will have to be decided eventually and the difficulty will be waiting. And a decision whose later part is undecided is not thereby easy to undo, since reversing a site after people have moved their plans towards it is harder than the original choice suggested.
questions.hint: Ask what is harder to settle and what the group gains by not settling it now.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: The decision a recommendation asks someone else to make
questions.learningObjective: distinguish recommending from deciding
questions.stem: A group's report ends by recommending that the funding body raise the grant. What has the group done?

options.text: Decided the matter, since a recommendation that goes unchallenged has settled the question
options.misconception: equates absence of dispute with agreement and treats advice as though it were binding

options.text: Ruled out the alternatives, since a report that names one option has by that fact dismissed the others
options.misconception: assumes naming a preference settles the question without any argument being made about the rest

options.text: Identified a preferred course and left the choice with the body that can make it, which is a contribution and not the same as a decision
Passed responsibility to the funding body, which is a way of avoiding having to decide
options.misconception: reads the allocation of a decision as evasion rather than as a choice about who is entitled to decide

questions.explanation: A recommendation is the group doing the part it is competent to do and naming where the rest of the decision lies. Putting a preferred course in a report is a substantive act and it commits the group to a preference, so it is not the neutral thing it can look like from the outside. What the group has not done is settle the question, because the funding body holds the power and the responsibility and will have to weigh the group's recommendation against considerations the group cannot see, such as what the same money would do elsewhere. Deciding who decides is therefore part of the work rather than a way of dodging it, and a report that leaves it unstated is the report that has most likely avoided deciding anything.
questions.hint: Ask who holds the power and the responsibility once the recommendation is written.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: The choice to keep an arrangement when advice is declined
questions.learningObjective: say what declining a recommendation amounts to
questions.stem: An advisory group recommends a change and the department it advises decides not to make it. What has the department done?

options.text: Rejected the evidence, since declining a recommendation shows the material behind it was not good enough
options.misconception: reads a declined recommendation as a verdict on the evidence rather than on the fit of the change

options.text: Exercised a decision that was always open to it, since advice binding nobody has to leave the choice with whoever holds it
Broken an undertaking, since a recommendation produced at such length ought to be carried out
options.misconception: treats advisory status as though it were an agreement the department entered into

options.text: Done nothing at all, since the existing arrangement stands and nothing has changed
options.misconception: equates an absence of change with an absence of a decision

questions.explanation: If a recommendation binds nobody, then the choice has to stay with whoever can make it, and that body has just made the choice not to change anything. That is a decision and it deserves the same treatment as any other: what it rests on, what it costs, and what would make it worth revisiting. Declining a recommendation is not a verdict on the evidence, because a department may hold perfectly good material and still judge the change unsuited to circumstances the advisory group did not examine. Nor is the existing arrangement a default, since it was put there by some earlier choice and continuing it is a further choice being made each year it continues.
questions.hint: Ask where the decision has to sit if the advice does not bind.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A consultation that reached a part of the population
questions.learningObjective: state what a consultation supports about those it did not reach

stimulus.kind: consultation record written for this question
stimulus.body: Consultation record written for this exercise, for one branch library. 'The branch has 214 registered members. The consultation reached 61 of them by email. Of the 61, 38 wrote a comment. 26 of those 38 wrote that the Saturday closure makes travel difficult, 9 wrote that the present hours suit them, and 3 wrote about neither. The branch has run its present hours for six years, and the lease on the building ends in 14 months.'

questions.stem: The group plans to write a sentence about what members think. What can this record support?

options.text: That most members find the Saturday closure difficult, since 26 of the 38 who commented wrote about it
options.misconception: treats a majority of the commenters as a majority of members and sets aside the 23 reached who stayed silent

options.text: That the present hours should be kept, since 9 members asked for them out of the 61 who were reached
options.misconception: makes the same substitution in the opposite direction, from a count of commenters to a verdict on members

options.text: That 26 of the 61 members reached reported a difficulty, and no claim about the 153 members who were never reached
That the consultation failed, since reaching 61 members out of 214 is too small a share to count for anything
options.misconception: discards a usable record on grounds of size rather than stating what the 61 respondents do support

questions.explanation: The record covers 61 of 214 members, so 153 were not reached at all, and it describes 38 of those 61 in their own words. What it supports is a statement about what 26 people reported, and that is worth making: 26 of 61 is not a small number of reported difficulties and it bears on whether the Saturday closure should stay. It supports nothing at all about the 153, and no amount of counting the 38 will change that, since the gap was made when the email list was shorter than the membership. The share who commented also cannot be turned into a verdict either way, because 23 of the 61 wrote nothing and they are not silent votes for the option they did not mention.
questions.hint: Subtract the members reached from the members on the roll, and then separate the commenters from the reached.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Triage when the deadline will not move
questions.learningObjective: state what a first stage of a rushed decision must identify

stimulus.kind: triage note written for this question
stimulus.body: Note written for this exercise. 'A funder's deadline is 10 days away. The group holds four candidate schemes: A, which the record supports and which cannot be started without a partner organisation; B, which the record supports and which the group can start alone; C, which the record does not support but which several members favour; and D, for which the record is silent and no one has looked. The decision is about which two to put to the funder, since only two may be submitted.'

questions.stem: The group has ten days and can submit two schemes. First say what the triage must identify about the four candidates; then say how the two are chosen. What must the first answer contain?

options.text: That only A and B are eligible, since a scheme the record does not support cannot be submitted at all
options.misconception: rules out the schemes on the strength of silence and so treats absence of support as disqualification

options.text: That the record supports A and B, is silent on C and D, so C is a preference the record has not addressed
That D should be investigated first, since it is the only candidate nobody has examined yet
options.misconception: prioritises the gap in the record and ignores that the deadline bounds the investigation too

options.text: That the four candidates are equivalent, since the group has not yet had time to tell them apart
options.misconception: treats the absence of a comparison as a finding that the candidates are alike

questions.explanation: The triage has to say what the record already does for each candidate and where it says nothing, because ten days is a bound on everything that follows and the group cannot spend it re-asking a question the record has answered. On this file it supports A and B, and on D it is silent, which is a different thing from having found nothing against D. That silence is precisely why C and D cannot be ranked alongside A and B on this record. The second stage then has a choice to make rather than a calculation: submit the two the record supports and say what was left out and why, or spend some of the ten days looking at D and submit A with D, in which case the submission must say what the look did not settle.
questions.hint: Ask which of the four the record has something to say about and which it is merely quiet on.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What makes a decision reviewable afterwards
questions.learningObjective: name what a record of a decision has to preserve
questions.stem: A group decides to close a service and later has to explain the decision. What does the record of that decision have to keep in order to be reviewable?

options.text: The names of everyone who voted for it, since a decision is only accountable if the members are identifiable
options.misconception: supposes accountability rests on names rather than on the grounds the decision was made on

options.text: A statement that the decision was unanimous, since a division in the room would weaken the decision
options.misconception: records unanimity as the thing worth having and passes over the grounds that would show whether it was sound

options.text: The text of the proposal that was adopted, since the decision should be read against the wording that carried it
options.misconception: keeps the winning document and omits the comparison that made it a choice rather than a preference

options.text: The criterion used, the option rejected and the evidence relied on, since a decision cannot be checked against a record that kept none of the three

questions.explanation: A decision is reviewable when a later reader can reconstruct what it was being weighed against. That needs three things: the criterion, since a decision with no criterion cannot be checked against anything; the option that was not taken, since most decisions look obvious only while the alternative is still unnamed; and the evidence relied on, since a decision is a claim about the world and not only a preference. Names and votes are worth keeping for their own sake but they do not make a decision checkable, because a well-attended division of a well-supported criterion produces a decision no later reader can fault. The adopted wording is evidence of one thing only, namely what was agreed, and not of why it was preferred.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader would need in order to rebuild the choice rather than merely date it.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Evidence that would have changed a decision
questions.learningObjective: state what a first answer about reversing a decision must identify

stimulus.kind: decision note written for this question
stimulus.body: Decision note written for this exercise. 'The group closed the branch reading room on the stated ground that attendance in the last four quarters had fallen below the number needed to cover the running cost. The note records that cost per session and the attendance figures for each of the four quarters. It does not record what the sessions were, who came to them, or whether the same people would have come at a different time of day.'

questions.stem: A member asks what would have changed the decision. First say what the note must identify for that question to have an answer; then say what the group should do with the answer. What must the first answer contain?

options.text: That the group decided on attendance and cost alone, so the evidence that would have changed it is about the sessions and who attended them
That nothing would have changed it, since the attendance figures were the basis of the decision and they have not changed
options.misconception: takes the basis of a decision to be immune to further evidence about the thing it was about

options.text: That a fall in attendance is a fall in demand, since attendance is what a service is for and there is no other measure
options.misconception: collapses one measure of use into the whole of demand and passes over what the sessions were

options.text: That the decision should be reopened, since a member asking what would have changed it shows the closure was wrong
options.misconception: treats a question about the decision as an argument that the decision was mistaken

questions.explanation: The first answer has to identify what the decision was actually made on, because a decision can only be reversed by evidence bearing on the ground it was given. Here the ground was attendance against running cost, and on that ground nothing has moved. The evidence that would have changed it is of another kind: what the sessions were for and who was in them, since a hall running the wrong sessions at the wrong hour shows an attendance figure that does not measure demand. That leads to the second stage, which is not to reopen the decision but to decide what the group now knows. If the sessions were misdirected the answer is a different arrangement, and if they were the ones members wanted then the closure stands and the falling numbers become a question about how the room was run.
questions.hint: Ask what the decision was made on, and then what the note does not say about that thing.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Deciding on the cost of delay rather than on the evidence
questions.learningObjective: recognise a decision justified by the price of waiting
questions.stem: A group acts while the evidence on the main question is still incomplete, and says it did so because waiting would have cost more than acting on what it had. What has it produced?

options.text: A decision the group cannot justify, since it acted before it had the evidence its own procedure required
options.misconception: treats the price of delay as no ground at all and applies the procedure without an exception

options.text: A decision with a second and separate warrant, since the cost of delay is a real ground and one the group is now relying on
A decision it will not have to revisit, since the cost of waiting has already been settled and the question is closed
options.misconception: assumes that paying the cost of delay closes the question rather than carrying the consequence forward

options.text: An outcome that shows the incomplete evidence was good enough after all, since acting on it worked out
options.misconception: argues from the result and so needs the case to have been made in advance

questions.explanation: There are two distinct warrants available and the group has used the second one. The first is that the evidence supports the action, which is what it would normally say, and the second is that the evidence is incomplete, the waiting has a price and the price exceeds the risk of being wrong. The second is a legitimate ground and it should be stated as one, because it changes what the group is doing: it is accepting a risk knowingly and in advance rather than claiming a support it does not have. Once it is stated, two consequences follow that the group's phrasing tends to hide. The incomplete evidence will not be repaired by the fact that the action went well, and the cost of waiting will be paid again on the next question unless the group decides each time whether to pay it.
questions.hint: Ask what the group is claiming, and whether the price of waiting is a second claim of its own.
